summary_responses.subtopic: Federal Credit Union Chartering & Associational Common Bond Rules
summary_responses.response: The National Credit Union Administration (NCUA) Board has issued a final rule (RIN 3133-AF93) amending its Chartering and Field of Membership Manual in 12 CFR part 701 to revise the criteria for determining associational common bonds, effective January 4, 2027. The rule clarifies that requiring members to purchase a good, product, or service as a condition of membership will no longer automatically disqualify a group from recognition as an association, eliminating the fraternal-insurance example that had been read as a categorical bar. NCUA retains its long-standing policy that associations based *primarily* on a client-customer relationship do not qualify, and will instead weigh the totality of a group's structure, purpose, and activities to decide whether the client-customer relationship is merely incidental. Of the 18 comments received on the April 8, 2026 proposal by the June 8, 2026 deadline, all but one—a bankers association that warned of eroding statutory field-of-membership limits and competitive equity—supported the change, and the Board responded to requests for clarity by detailing its review criteria, adding examples, and streamlining reviews of pre-approved groups. The amendments apply only to single associational charters and multiple common bond federal credit unions, not to occupational or community charters or federally insured state-chartered credit unions.

summary_responses.subtopic: Federal Reserve Regulation D & Depository Institution Reserve Requirements
summary_responses.response: The Federal Reserve Board has issued a final rule amending Regulation D (Reserve Requirements of Depository Institutions) to reflect the statutorily required annual indexing of the reserve requirement exemption amount and the low reserve tranche for 2027. Because total reservable liabilities at all depository institutions fell 2.4 percent (from $21,103 billion to $20,588 billion) between June 30, 2025, and June 30, 2026, the exemption amount stays unchanged at $39.2 million. Net transaction accounts rose 2.7 percent (from $17,012 billion to $17,465 billion) over the same period, so the low reserve tranche increases by $14.4 million to $688.5 million, effective for institutions beginning January 1, 2027, with the rule itself taking effect December 18, 2026. Since the Board set all reserve requirement ratios to zero in March 2020, these adjustments are purely ministerial and will not change institutions' actual reserve requirements, which remain zero. The Board therefore found good cause to skip notice and comment under the Administrative Procedure Act, and concluded that the Regulatory Flexibility Act's analysis requirements and any Paperwork Reduction Act collections do not apply.

summary_responses.response: On November 16, 2026, the SEC published notice of a proposed rule change filed by the Texas Stock Exchange LLC (TXSE) on November 10, 2026, seeking public comment on amendments to its fee schedule and Lead Market Maker (LMM) Program, with an intended implementation date of November 2, 2026. The Exchange proposes to raise the rebate for orders adding displayed liquidity in securities priced at or above $1.00 from $0.0031 to $0.0032 per share, while increasing the fee for adding or removing non-displayed liquidity in those securities from $0.0002 to $0.0006 per share and eliminating fees entirely for non-displayed executions in securities priced below $1.00. TXSE also proposes a new enhanced rebate of $0.0038 per share for members adding displayed liquidity in TXSE-listed corporate securities priced at or above $1.00, arguing that these pricing changes are competitively justified and will encourage displayed quoting, deeper liquidity, and better price discovery. In its LMM Program, launched in September 2026, the Exchange would redefine "Size Near the Inside" to require minimum notional value on both sides within 0.25% of the NBBO for at least 95% of the trading day, and redefine "Time at NBBO" as the average of the time spent quoting at least $10,000 notional at the NBB and at the NBO separately, accommodating legitimate inventory-driven quoting differences. Finally, TXSE would add notes excluding periods with missing, invalid, locked, or crossed SIP NBBO quotes from NBBO-referenced metric denominators and scaling certain percentage-based performance thresholds for leveraged ETPs by their leverage factor, and it asserts the proposal is consistent with Sections 6(b)(4) and 6(b)(5) of the Exchange Act as an equitable, reasonable, and non-discriminatory allocation of fees.

summary_responses.subtopic: Clearing Agency Capital Management & Securities Exchange Fee Holidays
summary_responses.response: The Options Clearing Corporation (OCC) filed a proposed rule change with the SEC on November 4, 2026, to implement a fee holiday for December 1–31, 2026, which took effect immediately upon filing, with the SEC publishing notice to solicit public comment. Under OCC's Commission-approved Capital Management Policy, when its liquid net assets funded by equity (LNAFBE) exceed 110% of its Target Capital Requirement—the "early warning" threshold—OCC may return excess capital to clearing members through measures such as fee holidays, as it did in December 2025. Strong clearing volumes in the first half of 2026, plus three fewer months of interest payments on members' margin cash than budgeted (payments began in October rather than July 2026), left OCC with capital well above that threshold and likely to stay there through 2027. The holiday would cut the clearing fee from $0.025 to $0.00 per contract effective December 1 and eliminate the $200 minimum monthly clearing fee once regulatory approvals are obtained, forgoing roughly $77 million in revenue while keeping LNAFBE above the 2026 threshold of $355.3 million and the projected 2027 threshold of $390.8 million under most volume scenarios; fees revert to prior levels on the first trading day of 2027. OCC argues the change satisfies Section 17A(b)(3)(D) of the Exchange Act's requirement for equitable allocation of reasonable fees, citing Board and SEC oversight, annual examinations, and its ongoing financial transparency through annual reports and quarterly disclosures, while still preserving capital adequate to its obligations as a systemically important financial market utility.

summary_responses.subtopic: Federal Electronic Payment Systems Modernization & Digital Fee Infrastructure
summary_responses.response: The Federal Aviation Administration has issued a notice of proposed rulemaking (Docket No. FAA-2026-3538) to modernize its payment systems by requiring electronic payments and eliminating paper methods such as cash, money orders, and paper checks. The proposal implements Executive Order 14247, "Modernizing Payments To and From America's Bank Account," which directs federal agencies to phase out paper receipts and disbursements in order to improve government efficiency. FAA would amend payment provisions in 14 CFR parts 13, 47, 49, 61, 63, 65, 187, and 406, covering civil penalties, aircraft registration and recording fees, duplicate airman and medical certificates and knowledge test reports, overflight fees, and services performed outside the United States, while still permitting alternative methods where otherwise authorized by law. Although FAA already directs customers to pay through Pay.gov in practice, several regulations list only paper options or allow both, so the rule would align the regulatory text and related advisory circulars (AC Forms 8050-1B, 8050-5, and 8060-56) with current electronic practice. FAA estimates annual cost savings of $99,815 (about $457,125 over five years at a three percent discount rate and $1,425,933 in perpetuity), considers customer transition costs de minimis, and is accepting public comments through January 4, 2027.

summary_responses.response: The FAA has issued a notice of proposed rulemaking (Docket No. FAA-2026-13819) that would adopt a new airworthiness directive for certain Airbus Helicopters Deutschland EC135 and EC635T2+ helicopters, covering all serial numbers up to and including 1276. The action was prompted by a finding that the manufacturer's master service manual lacks complete inspection instructions following a hard landing, which could allow tail rotor control damage to go undetected and lead to component failure and reduced control of the helicopter. summary_responses.response: The National Park Service has issued a final rule amending the special regulations for Mammoth Cave National Park in Kentucky, effective December 21, 2026. The rule authorizes the park superintendent to designate roughly 37 miles of multi-use trails for bicycle use, identifying 12 trails in total, including eight newly constructed trails such as the Crystal Cave Road, East Entrance, and Sugar Sink trails. Two trails currently open to bikes—the Maple Springs Connector Trail and the White Oak Trail—will be removed from the list, with the connector trail closed and restored to natural conditions. The rule also creates an exception to general NPS regulations barring horses on park roads by permitting equestrian use on the 5.4-mile Houchin Ferry North/Ollie Road, giving riders new loop options and access to the river. These changes implement part of the preferred alternative in the park's 2024 Comprehensive Land and River Trails Plan and Environmental Assessment, which received a Finding of No Significant Impact in December 2024 and would expand the park's trail system by about 66 miles while using sustainable construction techniques to protect natural and cultural resources.
